en: Choosing companions from their own kin.
This was Közkaman's plan,
That unbeliever who had seen much,
Honest outside, treacherous within.
Setting their course toward Manas,
The five men were going.
Reckoning it out in their minds,
The five pigs took their sons as companions.
Kökchököz's nine sons,
Közkaman's nine sons,
Zheltiibes's nine sons,
Changdyayak's nine sons,
Orozon's nine sons—
White tents when they camped upon the plain,
The utterly treacherous Kalmyks
Were traveling to Manas.
When they came midway,
They chose and provided a swift horse,
And sent a letter to dearly cherished Manas Khan.
If you look at the letter they sent,
The five wrote words in tears:
'Leopard Manas, dear lion,
At root we are your kin,' they wrote.
'When your grandfather, hero Karakan, died,
The plundering of a khan's estate was a grievous affair.
The great Kyrgyz and Oigut people,
With the Russians coming from the right,
Were hemmed in by two khans
And divided as booty.
When our poor lives endured humiliation,
When they plundered our possessions,
When they wrought havoc,
Whoever spoke back,
The two khans seized
And slaughtered as a sacrifice.
When they imposed heavy tribute,
The Kyrgyz people, exhausted,
Wandered away in every direction.
I turned and looked, yet did not die;
Thus we have reached our wish.
The Kyrgyz along the road were slaughtered;
We wandered away to Beijing.
We wandered, entered, and survived.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
We survived by tending their children.
King Manas, take heed,
The countless cattle bred in our herds
We scattered and came wandering,
Through deserts where no bird flies,
Through passes where no dog treads,
We come lost and wandering.
Ridden to Altai, you would not tire;
Calling you our courser, we come wandering.
We share a father and a faith;
Calling you kin, we come wandering.
Rubbing your calves raw,
With all our hearts in pain,
Calling you kin, we come wandering.
The Kalmyks attacked my migration;
Against the Black Manchus and Sibe
I departed unable to take revenge.
The monks shattered my migration;
Against the uncomprehending Jurchen,
Come, leopard Manas,
I come unable to take revenge.
My fat is gone, my bones remain;
I am wasting away.
'When will I see my Manas?'
I am growing old as I go.
The torment of this world,
I am experiencing as I go.
My wits flee, my strength departs;
Unable to see you, my king,
I am dying as I go.
Only a spoonful of my blood remains;
My flesh has hardened, all lean and dark.
My one magnanimous Manas,
I am coming to see you.
Then Karakan's eight sons
Were all left young and playful,
Left sprawled upon their bellies, dazed.
Driven by warriors, crossing waters,
Karakan's eight sons
Were driven on until few remained.
Your strides became known to the people;
When they heard of your spiritual might,
The khakan's people grieved.
Your name reached this place,
Inscribed in Karykan's register.
You prospered, endowed with spiritual might;
Hero, you were born and grew in Altai.
While I lived in Beijing,
I gathered what the learned men passed down;
I questioned those who knew.
I lived in slavery and traveled long.
Beside the dauntless leopard Manas,
Escaping from the unbelievers,
I longed to settle my household.
You exhausted my treasury and possessions
I scatter it and depart.
My Prophet is true, my faith is true;
We are all of Kyrgyz stock.
Manas, my younger brother, receive me;
I am fleeing toward you.'
They sent a carefully fashioned letter
To the guileless leopard Manas,
Delivering it swiftly to stir his grief.
Speaking words that reached the marrow,
Of open-hearted Manas
They burned the heart with forceful words:
'I am your kin, of one blood;
Let my Manas receive me,' they said.
Tied tightly upon their crowns,
With fur caps worn over them,
If we looked at the five champions,
Unknown to any other person,
They had topknots upon their heads.
Among the five Kalmyks
Was the head of a blue-gray pig.
The open-hearted Manas
They planned to deceive and slaughter.
The golden throne in Beijing,
They spoke of somehow mounting it.
Your guileless only one, Manas—
If they could somehow lay hands on him,
They would secretly put him to death.
Six swift horses came;
To your unfortunate mother's white palace,
With its gates of iron and white tin,
A palm-sized letter came.
When we read and examined it,
Your father's name was there.
The five swine wrote a tearful letter:
“If his heroism is true,
Let the renowned leopard Manas
Come out to welcome us,” they wrote.
Yesterday, my son, in the Zhylyngduu valley,
Along the broad Talas,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz, choosing the lowland,
Were encamped together;
By day, kumys, by night, girls—
Such was their life then.
Your ill-fated mother, gifted with foresight,
Wept in sorrow and alarm.
Within that great assembly,
Mighty Bakai read out
The letter that had come, with fitting skill.
The Köng-Kol valley, the great Talas—
I knew it was a mountain.
From the wretch who lived among the Kalmyks
I knew an enemy had come.
I knew that Karykan's golden throne
Had been received;
United as your father's enemies,
They had dug a deep, broad pit—
I knew they had prepared it.
I, your mother Kanykei,
My heart sorely distracted,
The tears pouring from my eyes,
Saw Kökchököz and Közkaman
Revealed as enemies.
Weeping and beating myself,
To your guileless father Manas
I pleaded long:
“Your courser has come exhausted;
Your hungry kinsman has come.
For forty years, in Chinese Beijing,
He has settled as their neighbor.
The wretch's heart will never turn;
He has openly become Chinese.
Can one called Kökchököz prosper?
Can there be one called Közkaman?
For an upright, pure Muslim soul,
Could the name of a woodland pig
Ever be bestowed?
Good heavens, can a Muslim be like this?
If he were truly a Muslim,
Would he bear a pig's name?
Good heavens, can one called Közkaman prosper?
Your Kalmyk with his corrupt name,
If he settles beside you,
Will he openly be a kinsman?
If he survives, my blood-shedding hero,
Your gold will count for less than coal.
If that accursed man settles beside you,
Once fattened, he will forget what he received.
My silver will count for less than coal.
Your hulking, accursed Kalmyk,
Once fattened, will not know your anguish.
Your fine silk will count for less than felt;
Once clothed, he will not know your worth.
Your silk will count for less than felt;
Once clothed, he will not know your anguish.
Can a Kalmyk be your kin?
That accursed man of the dark faith—
Can it be right to call him kin?
When your Kalmyk grows fat,
Will he not demand to be an equal kinsman?
When he comes spurring on his horse,
Will he not eat your well-fed foal?
He will seize and break your spear;
Once fattened, kicking out,
He will leave you helpless.
Once he has learned your secrets,
Will he not hollow you out and devour you?
When you come spurring against each other,
Will your Kalmyk not demand to be an equal kinsman?
If that Kalmyk settles beside you,
Will he not break into your treasury?
If you fall within his reach,
Will he not cut off your head?
When those dogs turn against you,
Will they not push your door open?
Once they have eaten their fill, just wait—
Will they not scatter thick torment about?
There will be malice in your eyes;
There will be evasions in your words.
If your Kalmyk has the strength,
He will seek to strike you down.
There will be deceit in his words;
If your Kalmyk finds his chance,
He will seek to do you harm.
When he comes to this Talas,
He will ruin your encampment.
If those men have the strength,
They will wipe away all trace of you.
That Kalmyk is thinking
Of coming to settle in Talas.
Their desire is
To kill you, my king,
And become khan of Beijing.
If they come to this place,
It will be to bring calamity.
If those men survive,
They will kill you here,
Then go to Karykan of Beijing
To claim their reward for the glad news.
My generous lord, heed my words;
Understand the one thing I have told you!
They will strip off your robe and wear it.
Those men, keeping you apart,
Will bring strange suffering upon your head.
If they can, to the khagan
They will take you with your hands bound.
You have not accepted what I said.
You are determined to go, my sultan,
To the place where you will die in grief.
No good comes from the Kalmyks;
Their tidings are ill.
They should never settle beside us!
If they survive, you will see:
They will learn your secrets thoroughly.
If, grown strong, you will not heed me,
They will put an end to your quarrel.
They will watch your camp from afar.
If they survive, just wait—
